title: The beggar's song
hookLine: an old beggar's bowl is snatched from his hands, and he answers with a song that won't even blame karma
carry: not them, not karma: the mind turns the wheel
last: ACTION FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.

cards: A begging bowl, snatched out of an old man's hands. His staff, taken. His water pot, gone.
Someone throws dirt at him; someone spits. Krishna tells this story when Uddhava admits how hard it is to bear the insults of others.
The old man was once rich, a brahmin from Avanti, and a miser who never enjoyed his money or gave any of it away. Then, piece by piece, it was gone. Something turned in him.
He left home as a wandering beggar, and the people of the town made sport of him. What he says back is a song, and it refuses to blame anyone you'd expect.

teach.h: NOT THEM, NOT THE GODS, NOT KARMA.
teach.b: The song is sometimes called the Bhikshu Gita, the beggar's song. Its center, in paraphrase: these people aren't the cause of my joy and sorrow. Nor are the gods, nor my body, nor the planets, nor my karma, nor time.
The mind turns the wheel. Look who's on that list. Karma.
Plenty of people say "it's my karma" when life goes wrong, as if karma were a verdict. The beggar isn't saying karma isn't real. He's saying the place where sorrow gets made is closer than that.
Then he takes the list apart, one suspect at a time. If other people are the cause, it's one body knocking against another; what does the self, the atman, have to do with it?

teach.h: TEETH THAT BITE YOUR OWN TONGUE.
teach.b: When your own teeth bite your own tongue, who is there to be angry at? If the gods are the cause, what does that have to do with a self that doesn't change?

teach.h: THE ATMAN ISN'T WHAT GOT SHOVED.
teach.b: This is a big Hindu teaching in a small song: the atman, who you really are, isn't the thing that got shoved and spat on. The mind takes the blow and spins the wheel of joy and sorrow.

Many teachers read it this way: karma explains what arrives at your door, but the mind decides what it becomes inside. That's Krishna's answer to Uddhava about bearing hard words. Not pretending they didn't hurt.
Looking at where the hurt is being made.

how: The song of the brahmin of Avanti, sometimes called the Bhikshu Gita, is read by students of the Bhagavata's eleventh book as a teaching on bearing insult and on the mind as the source of joy and sorrow.

o: action, though the beggar names the mind as cause
a vow of poverty a wandering beggar takes
the alms placed into a beggar's bowl

games.q: the beggar's song — tap the pairs.
p: snatch his bowl and mock him
the mind causes joy and sorrow
then who is there to be angry at?

s: the beggar blames his karma for his suffering
karma is on his list of things he won't blame. he names the mind.
the man in the story used to be rich
a brahmin of Avanti, rich and miserly, until his wealth was lost.
Krishna tells the story when Uddhava admits insults are hard to bear
the beggar's song is Krishna's answer to that admission.

games.q: you're the old beggar. people snatch your bowl, throw dirt and mock you. what do you do?
o: curse them and everyone they love.
sing that they aren't the cause of your sorrow; the mind is.
go home and try to get rich again.
games.why: he sings: not these people, not the gods, not the body, the planets, karma or time. the mind is the cause.

practice: Bring to mind one small sorrow from this week and walk the beggar's list slowly: was it them, the day, your body, your luck?

Give each suspect its moment, then come to the last stop, your own mind, and simply watch what it's doing with that sorrow, without fixing it. If you pray, you can bring that mind, just as it is, to the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Karma. In the beggar's song even karma isn't blamed: the mind is named as the place where joy and sorrow turn.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a mendicant, one who lives on alms; the old brahmin becomes one, and his song is called the Bhikshu Gita.

carryVoice: Your line: not them, not karma: the mind turns the wheel. That's where the work can start. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.23.1–41 (Uddhava on how hard insults are to bear; the miserly brahmin of Avanti loses his wealth, becomes a mendicant and is mistreated)
Bhagavata Purana 11.23.42–57 (the mendicant's song: not people, gods, body, planets, karma or time, but the mind is the cause; the tongue bitten by one's own teeth)
Bhagavata Purana 11.23.58–61 (Krishna's closing words on the song)
